[[Category:Large language models]]
[[Category:Natural language processing]]

A '''large language model''' ('''LLM''') is an [[artificial intelligence]] system built as a [[neural network]] with a very large parameter count, typically based on the [[Transformer]] architecture, trained by [[machine learning]] on broad text corpora to generate text in response to prompts.<ref>{{#cite:Q3130}}</ref>

== Architecture ==

At the time of writing (2026-08), the most widely adopted LLMs are [[Transformer]] models, specifically [[autoregressive decoder-only Transformer]]s.<ref>{{#cite:Q3130}}</ref>

== Scaling laws ==

The performance of LLMs improves predictably with

* model size
* training-data volume
* computational budget

These regularities are the '''scaling laws'''.<ref>{{#cite:Q3141}}</ref> The [[language model loss]] falls as a power law in compute $F$ with an exponent near $0.05$, so diminishing returns are intrinsic. The [[Chinchilla prescription]] sets the compute-optimal balance between parameters and data at roughly 20 tokens per parameter,<ref>{{#cite:Q3164}}</ref> and the finite supply of high-quality public text places a practical ceiling on data scaling, with estimates suggesting a “data wall” may arrive by the late 2020s.<ref>{{#cite:Q3181}}</ref>

== Inference ==

At inference time, an LLM generates text by repeatedly sampling or selecting a token according to the conditional distribution $P(x_t \mid x_{1:t-1}; \theta)$ and appending it to the context. Decoding strategies such as greedy search, beam search, temperature sampling, and top-$p$ (nucleus) sampling trade off diversity against coherence.<ref>{{#cite:Q3198}}</ref> The computational cost of self-attention grows quadratically with context length, motivating techniques such as [[KV caching]] and efficient attention variants.<ref>{{#cite:Q3130}}</ref>

For a context of length $T$, causal [[self-attention]] computes a $T\times T$ score matrix, so its time and memory costs scale as

$$
\mathcal{O}(T^2d)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathcal{O}(T^2),
$$

respectively, where $d$ is the hidden dimension. [[KV caching]] removes redundant recomputation of past keys and values during autoregressive decoding, reducing the per-token attention cost from $\mathcal{O}(T^2d)$ to $\mathcal{O}(Td)$, at the expense of storing $2Td$ cached scalars per layer.<ref>{{#cite:Q3192}}</ref>

At each decoding step, a token is sampled from

$$
x_t \sim P(x_t\mid x_{1:t-1}; \theta).
$$

Temperature sampling replaces $P$ by

$$
P_\tau(x_t\mid x_{1:t-1})
=
\frac{\exp(z_{x_t}/\tau)}
{\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(z_v/\tau)},
$$

where $z_v$ is the logit assigned to vocabulary entry $v\in\mathcal{V}$, and $\tau>0$ is the temperature. Top-$p$ (nucleus) sampling restricts the support to the smallest set $\mathcal{S}_p$ such that

$$
\sum_{x\in\mathcal{S}_p}
P(x\mid x_{1:t-1})
\ge p.
$$
